makurakotoba.precedes: 富士の高嶺 (snow-covered peak, white things)
makurakotoba.conventional_meaning: white cloth/mulberry-bark cloth; conventionally precedes words for white things such as garments, sleeves, snow, clouds

jokotoba.text: 田子の浦に打ち出でてみれば
jokotoba.function: Establishes the speaker's physical movement out onto the open shore of Tago and the act of looking, which grammatically and narratively leads into the revelation of Fuji's snow-capped peak in the shimo-no-ku. This is not a fixed epithet but a scene-setting preface composed specifically for this poem's journey/vista structure.

honkadori.source_poem: 田子の浦ゆ うち出でて見れば 真白にぞ 富士の高嶺に 雪は降りける (Man'yōshū, Yamabe no Akahito, original longer form)
honkadori.echoed_phrase: 田子の浦に打ち出でてみれば...富士の高嶺に雪はふりつつ
honkadori.function: This Hyakunin Isshu version is itself a condensed/adapted quotation of Akahito's own Man'yōshū poem, substituting 真白にぞ...降りける with 白妙の...ふりつつ, shifting from a completed past state to an ongoing continuous image; the Hyakunin Isshu compilers selected this reworded Shin Kokinshū variant as canonical for the anthology.

kigo.note: Snow (雪) is the canonical winter kigo, evoking purity, stillness, and the sublime remoteness of the sacred mountain; here it also signals eternal or perpetual snow atop Fuji, a marker of the mountain's numinous, timeless quality rather than a fleeting seasonal storm.

bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker travels out onto the open shore of Tago Bay and looks up, an act of physical emergence and vision
bipartite.shimo_theme: The sublime, snow-covered peak of Mount Fuji is revealed in the distance, snow perpetually falling upon it
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku enacts the physical and perceptual act of stepping into open view and looking (打ち出でてみれば), which grammatically and dramatically discharges directly into the shimo-no-ku's revelation of Fuji's white peak — the entire poem hinges on the moment of sight transitioning from anticipation to the awe-inspiring visual object itself.

source_jp:
田子の浦に
打ち出でてみれば
白妙の
富士の高嶺に
雪はふりつつ
